steps.question: Chloe's rule: "If a cell is full of honey, then it is sealed with wax." Which cell would prove the rule FALSE?

lines: p: The cell is full of honey.
q: The cell is sealed with wax.

options.text: A full cell that is not sealed
An empty cell that is sealed
options.whyWrong: Here p is false. The rule only promises something about full cells, so an empty cell can't break it. When p is false, p → q is true.

options.text: An empty cell that is not sealed
options.whyWrong: Here p is false too, so the rule makes no claim about this cell. When p is false, p → q is true.

options.text: A full cell that is sealed
options.whyWrong: Here p and q are both true. This cell agrees with the rule, so p → q is true.

steps.hint: A conditional only makes a promise when p is true. Look for the cell where p is true but q is false.

polya.understand: p is "the cell is full of honey" and q is "the cell is sealed with wax". The rule is p → q.
polya.plan: Go through the four cases (p true or false, q true or false). Which one breaks the promise?
polya.lookBack: Only p true and q false makes p → q false. In the other three cases the conditional is true.

steps.explanation: A conditional p → q is false in only one case: p is true and q is false. A full cell that isn't sealed breaks the rule. If the cell isn't full, p is false, and the conditional is true no matter what, because the rule says nothing about empty cells.
steps.why: All mathematical propositions can be written as conditionals, so knowing when "if p, then q" is false is how mathematicians test a claim.

steps.question: Ethan's true statement: "If it is a honeybee cell, then it is a hexagon." Which statement is ALSO always true?

lines: p: It is a honeybee cell.

options.text: If it is not a hexagon, it is not a honeybee cell
If it is a hexagon, then it is a honeybee cell
options.whyWrong: That's the converse, q → p. A dragonfly's eye is made of hexagons but isn't a honeybee cell, so the converse is false.

options.text: If it is not a honeybee cell, it is not a hexagon
options.whyWrong: That's the inverse, ~p → ~q. A snowflake isn't a honeybee cell, but it has a hexagon shape, so the inverse is false.

options.text: It is a honeybee cell and it is not a hexagon
options.whyWrong: This says p is true and q is false, which is exactly the case that would make the original statement false.

steps.hint: Flip the statement around AND negate both parts. Which option does that?

polya.understand: The conditional is p → q. Its relatives are the converse (q → p), the inverse (~p → ~q), and the contrapositive (~q → ~p).
polya.plan: Name each option as converse, inverse, or contrapositive. Then try to find a counterexample for each.
polya.lookBack: A conditional and its contrapositive are equivalent, so if one is true, so is the other. The converse and inverse can be false.

steps.explanation: "If it is not a hexagon, then it is not a honeybee cell" is the contrapositive, ~q → ~p, and a conditional and its contrapositive are always equivalent. The converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other but not to the original, and here both are false: dragonfly eyes and snowflakes have hexagon shapes without being honeybee cells.
steps.why: Assuming the converse or inverse is true is one of the most common mistakes in everyday arguments.
